summary: We built a free web app that answers one question for the Moon's south pole: if a solar robot lands here on this day, does it survive 14 days? It is made for students in Kyrgyzstan and Central Asia: in English, Russian and Kyrgyz, with a ready 45 minute lesson, replays of real landings such as Chandrayaan-3 and IM-1, and four games on the real model, where a student builds a lander, keeps its battery alive, hunts for ice and takes a quiz. For planners it compares 15 sites near the south pole, or any point you add, on any day from 2021 to 2031, using NASA LOLA terrain and JPL ephemerides: a 3D Moon, the view from the ground with the Sun and Earth where they really are, and a calendar of which days work. Every landing gets one of three answers: GO, NOT SURE with a rate from 25 to 100%, or DON'T GO. The rate is the share of four re-checks (a day earlier, a day later, terrain 0.2° higher and lower) that give the other answer. Sites are ranked by a score, 8 spots 1 km around the target are judged, and a line says which Deep Space Network dish sees the Moon. Our Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to 0.0047 degrees. It matters because a launch that slips by one day can turn a safe landing into a lost one, and students here can now see why in their own language.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. Pick one of 15 sites near the Moon's south pole, or add any point by coordinates, and any day from 2021 to 2031. The app judges a 14 day stay of a solar robot hour by hour: night no longer than 2 days, radio silence no longer than 3 days, first sunlight within 24 hours, landing slope under 10 degrees (a NASA Artemis III rule). It shows a 3D Moon, the view from the ground with the Sun and Earth where they really are, and a calendar where each landing day is green (survives), red (lost) or yellow (not sure). Every landing gets GO, NOT SURE with a rate, or DON'T GO: the rate is the share of four re-checks (a day earlier, a day later, terrain 0.2° higher and lower) that give the other answer. Sites are ranked by a score (green days divided by all days, times 100). A compass judges 8 spots 1 km around the target. A line says which NASA Deep Space Network dish (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra) sees the Moon. Real landings (Chandrayaan-3, IM-1, Chang'e 6, IM-2) can be replayed.

FOR STUDENTS. English, Russian and Kyrgyz. Four games on the real model: build your own lander, keep its battery alive, hunt for ice, take a quiz. A ready 45 minute lesson.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS RIGHT. Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to 0.0047 degrees at worst. At Chandrayaan-3's site the model's sunset is 4 September 2023, the day ISRO put the lander to sleep. Automated tests cover the planner and the games.

LIMITS WE STATE. Terrain is 80 m (320 m for points you add and for the 1 km check). The night, radio and first sunlight limits are our teaching values; 0.2° and the 10° dish value are our own test values, not NASA figures. The score is a share of days, not a science score. Our sunlight on ridges runs about 11 points high against NASA's maps. The dish line is geometry only.

TOOLS. JavaScript, three.js, astronomy-engine, Python (Skyfield, NumPy, jplephem), Playwright tests, Firebase Hosting, Claude as a coding assistant.

Code and full description: https://github.com/pathmaker7/404-llsn
